Annotation Interface Derives

@Retention(SOURCE) @Target(TYPE) public @interface Derives
Asks the forj plugin to derive type class instances for a record: what record User(long id, String name) derives Codec { } compiles to. Written by hand it is the plain-Java spelling: @Derives(Codec.class) record User(long id, String name) { }.

For each type class X listed, the record gets a given X<User> named after the type class (codec for Codec), built through a convention X declares:

  • Required, the generic form: a static field(String name, Function<T, F> getter) that takes using X<F>, and a static product(Function<Object[], T> constructor, <field type>... fields). The derived instance is X.product(a -> new User((long) a[0], (String) a[1]), X.<User, Long>field("id", u -> u.id()), ...). Each component's instance is resolved like any using argument, so givens in scope (a custom X<Instant>) apply.
  • Optional, the specialized form: a static deriveProduct(constructor, encoder, fields...) and deriveField(out, index, value) overloads. forj then also generates the encoder as straight-line code, X.deriveField(out, 0, u.id()); X.deriveField(out, 1, u.name()); ..., and javac's overload resolution picks the deriveField for each component's type (a long one avoids boxing). A deriveField taking using X<A> covers every other type.
forj knows nothing about what X does; the convention is all it uses.
